Tics and Tic Disorders

1Illness script
Bottom line
  • 2 or more motor tics 1 or more vocal tics, at least 1 year, onset before 18 Tourette syndrome; echolalia counts as vocal
  • Repeated act no obsession behind it a tic, not a compulsion
  • No impairment explain and watch. Impairment CBIT (comprehensive behavioral intervention for tics) an alpha-2 agonist for milder tics, especially with ADHD (attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder) an antipsychotic for severe tics, aripiprazole first
What it is

Sudden, rapid, nonrhythmic movements or sounds

Tourette: 2 or more motor 1 or more vocal tics for at least 1 year, onset before 18

Driver

Cause unknown runs in families (in some, dominant with incomplete penetrance)

Triggers

Family history non-modifiable male sex (about 3 boys to 1 girl) non-modifiable

Worse with stress fatigue downtime

Chain

Urge (in some) tic; some can hold it back for seconds to minutes

Onset typically at 4 to 6 peak at 10 to 12 lessens in adolescence some persist

Insights

ADHD OCD (obsessive-compulsive disorder) often impair more than the tics screen every patient

Tics ADHD a stimulant is still allowed; watch for new or worse tics

What tics do, stage by stagedetail behind the chain
Each ticSome feel an urge first; some can hold a tic back for seconds to minutes; fewer during focused tasks, usually none in sleep
ChildhoodOnset before 18, usually at 4 to 6 years; tics wax and wane
PeakMost severe at about 10 to 12 years
AdolescenceTics lessen in many
AdulthoodMost tics eventually go away on their own; in a minority they persist into adulthood
ComorbidityADHD is the most common; OCD is common too; both often interfere more than the tics
StimulantsA stimulant can bring out or worsen tics in some children, yet tics do not rule one outin trials of children with tics and ADHD, methylphenidate did not worsen tics on average
3Differential
Look-alikes, most tempting first
DiagnosisFingerprintDecides it
Tourette syndromeTwo or more motor tics plus one or more vocal tics, not always at the same time1 year or more; both motor and vocal tics
Obsessive-compulsive disorderIntrusive thoughts drive repeated acts that relieve the distressA named obsession; a tic neutralizes none. The two often coexist
Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorderInattention or hyperactivity in 2 or more settings6 months or more, some before age 12; often coexists with tics
Angry or irritable mood, argument and defiance, vindictiveness6 months or more of defiance, not an involuntary movement
Persistent (chronic) tic disorderMotor or vocal tics, not both1 year or more, only one type
Provisional tic disorderMotor and/or vocal ticsUnder 1 year
Stereotypies (stereotypic movements)Repetitive, usually bilateral, such as hand flapping; with autism or intellectual disability, or in typical young childrenRhythmic, where a tic is not; distraction, such as calling the child's name, stops it
Rapid, irregular jerks, often spreading to the feet and face; may unmask OCDOften months after a strep infection; a major criterion of rheumatic fever
PANDAS (pediatric autoimmune neuropsychiatric disorder associated with streptococcal infections), a contested labelRare: tics or obsessive-compulsive symptoms of explosive onset after a strep infectionExplosive onset: tics constant within a day, after a strep infection
A drug, medication or medical causeTic-like movements with a culprit drug (eg, methylphenidate) or a condition such as seizures, Huntington disease or postviral encephalitisThe culprit drug or the other condition is found
4Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext move
Repeats exactly what other children sayEcholalia, a vocal ticCounts toward Tourette syndrome
Shrugs, turns the head, raises a hand again and again, with no obsessionMotor ticsNot OCD treatment
One tic fades and another appearsThe waxing and waning courseExpected; the diagnosis stands
Concerns reported from school aloneOnly 1 setting so farConfirm a second setting before calling it ADHD

Pause point. The bait: a 7-year-old referred from school for behavior, whose father has OCD. OCD is common alongside tics, but a relative's diagnosis does not describe this child's movements. With no obsession, his repeated acts are tics, so exposure and response prevention and an SSRI (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor) miss the target. He is bullied and isolated, so the tics impair, and treatment is warranted.

5Diagnostic criteria
Defining criteria: tic disorders Tourette – two or more motor tics and one or more vocal tics, not always at the same time; tics for at least 1 year · Persistent (chronic) – motor or vocal tics, not both, for 1 year or more · Provisional – motor and/or vocal tics for less than 1 year · All three – onset before 18; not due to a medication or drug, or another medical condition (eg, seizures, Huntington disease, postviral encephalitis)
Tic types
TypeMotorVocal
Simple: brief, no social meaningBlinking, grimacing, head jerking, shoulder shruggingGrunting or barking, sniffing or snorting, throat clearing
Complex: longer, may look intentionalCombined simple tics (head turning plus shrugging); echopraxia, imitating movements; copropraxia, obscene gesturesEcholalia, repeating another person's sounds or words, or one's own; coprolalia, socially inappropriate words
Clinical diagnosis: no test confirms it
6Severity
Impairment sets the plan
SituationChoose
Tics with no functional impairmentExplain the natural history; watchful waiting
Tics that significantly interfere with activities or self-imageTreat the tics: behavioral therapy (CBIT) first
ADHD or OCD that impairsTreat it too; it often impairs more than the tics
7Treatment
1

Explainevery patient

Psychoeducation on the natural history

Without functional impairment, watchful waiting is enough. Guideline detailRefer teachers and peers to psychoeducation resources.

2

1st linetics interfere with activities or self-image

Behavioral therapy: What it isComprehensive behavioral intervention for tics: cognitive-behavioral therapy built around habit reversal training, which teaches a replacement behavior for each tic.

Offer it before medication when it is available.

3

Addmild to moderate tics, especially with ADHD

An alpha-2 agonist: MechanismA central alpha-2 adrenergic agonist (also imidazoline receptors): lowers sympathetic outflow from the brain.Watch for sedation, low blood pressure and a slow heart rate; stopping it suddenly can cause rebound hypertension. or guanfacine

With ADHD, it may help both.

Check heart rate and blood pressure; taper to stop
4

Escalatetics are harder to control

An MechanismSecond-generation drugs block D2 dopamine and 5-HT2A serotonin receptors; aripiprazole is instead a D2 partial agonist. First-generation drugs carry significant extrapyramidal effects.Watch for drug-induced movement disorders; weight gain (risperidone, aripiprazole); high prolactin from D2 blockade (haloperidol, pimozide, risperidone). Aripiprazole raises prolactin less. Pimozide or ziprasidone: an ECG (electrocardiogram) for the QTc (the interval from the Q wave to the end of the T wave, corrected for heart rate) before and after starting.: aripiprazole first

Risperidone also reduces tics; haloperidol and pimozide are kept for severe, resistant tics. Beyond the ladderDeep brain stimulation for an adult with severe tics after, or unable to take, several drug classes and CBIT; multidisciplinary review first.
Botulinum toxin for a localized simple motor tic in an adolescent or adult; weakness and a soft voice, all temporary.
Tetrabenazine blocks VMAT2 (vesicular monoamine transporter type 2); increasingly used off-label; drowsiness, depression, parkinsonism.

Lowest effective dose
First treatment by situation
SituationChooseWatch for
Tics impair, no ADHDCBIT; then an alpha-2 agonist for milder tics, an antipsychotic for severe onesAlpha-2 agonist: heart rate, blood pressure, taper to stop. Antipsychotic: lowest effective dose; movement and metabolic effects
Tics impair, with ADHDCBIT; then clonidine or guanfacine, which may help bothStop an alpha-2 agonist by taper: rebound hypertension
The ADHD is what impairsTreat the ADHD; tics do not rule out a stimulantTics can emerge or worsen in some: lower the dose, or switch to atomoxetine or an alpha-2 agonist
Tics with OCDAn SSRI plus exposure and response prevention for the OCD; the tic plan as usualExposure therapy targets compulsions; a tic neutralizes no obsession
8Follow-up
Follow-up decisions
WhenDo
Tics for under 1 yearFollow over time: that is how Tourette syndrome separates from tics that pass
Every visitExpect waxing and waning; many improve in adolescence
On an alpha-2 agonistCheck heart rate and blood pressure; taper to stop
On an antipsychotic Lowest effective dose; watch for movement, metabolic and hormonal effects; taper over weeks to months to stop
ADHD that impairsMake sure the ADHD is treated
Practice
  1. 7 yo M with head turning, shoulder shrugging and repetition of classmates' words for over a year, now bullied and socially isolated → Risperidone → Tourette syndrome that impairs him; with CBIT, an alpha-2 agonist and aripiprazole not among the options, risperidone, which also reduces tics, is the best choice offered
  2. 8 yo M with mild motor and vocal tics who is performing well academically and has friends → Reassurance and education about the natural history → tics that do not impair need no tic treatment: explain the waxing and waning course and watch; habit reversal training waits until tics interfere
  3. 9 yo M with motor tics who also describes intrusive thoughts of contamination relieved only by repeated handwashing → Comorbid obsessive-compulsive disorder → a tic disorder alone has no obsession behind the act; contamination thoughts relieved by handwashing are an obsession and a compulsion, treated with exposure and response prevention
  4. 7 yo M with head jerking and eye blinking for 8 months and no vocal tic → Provisional tic disorder → tics for under 1 year are provisional, whether motor, vocal or both; Tourette syndrome and persistent (chronic) tic disorder need 1 year
  5. How antipsychotic agents suppress tics in Tourette syndrome → Dopamine receptor blockade → tetrabenazine instead depletes presynaptic dopamine
  6. 8 yo with Tourette syndrome and inattention impairing him at home and at school → A stimulant for the comorbid ADHD → stimulants are not contraindicated in Tourette syndrome; on average, methylphenidate treats the ADHD without worsening tics, though tics can emerge or worsen in some children (American Academy of Neurology guideline, 2019)
  7. 7 yo with Tourette syndrome whose parents request medication to reduce the tics → Fluoxetine → a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) treats comorbid OCD, not tics
  8. 10 yo with moderate impairing tics whose parents decline an antipsychotic because of weight-gain concerns → Guanfacine → for moderate tics an alpha-2 agonist is a first-line medication and comes before an antipsychotic, which is second line
Pairs with School Difficulty in a Child is the nearest relative. It shares the same referral route, a school behavior complaint. The resolution is opposite: there the private interview reveals a learning disorder, and here the examination reveals tics. Ask: what exactly is the child doing, and is it involuntary?
Transferable rule A family history raises the prior probability, but the phenomenology decides. When a relative's diagnosis and a child's behavior are both given, first describe the behavior in neutral terms. If the behavior is involuntary and stereotyped, it is a tic, whatever the family carries.
Common wrong answers For a school-age child with motor and vocal tics who is referred from school and whose father has OCD: Exposure and response prevention: the father's OCD makes it tempting, but it treats compulsions driven by obsessions, and the child describes no obsession. Fluoxetine: an SSRI is a first-line medication for OCD, but it treats obsessions and compulsions, not tics. Parent management training: it treats oppositional defiant disorder, a pattern of defiance, and does nothing for involuntary movements. Methylphenidate or atomoxetine: ADHD often coexists with tics, but these movements are tics, and concerns reported from school alone do not meet the 2-setting criterion for ADHD.
